lessons.title: Pick-and-roll anatomy
lessons.objective: Name the ball handler, screener, roll, pop and slip.

payload.prompt: What is a pick-and-roll?

options.text: A ball handler uses a screen set by a teammate, then either drives or the screener rolls to the basket.
A player without the ball sets a screen for a teammate cutting to the basket.
The referee calls a pick foul followed by a jump ball.

explanation.correct: The pick-and-roll is one of the most common actions in basketball: a screen for the ball handler, then the screener rolls to the rim while the handler drives or shoots. Two defenders must decide what to do.
explanation.incorrect: The pick-and-roll is a screen set for the player with the ball, not for a cutter. After the screen, the screener rolls toward the rim, and the handler can drive, shoot or pass.

payload.prompt: After the screen, the screener sprints to the rim for a lob. Roll or pop?

scene.alt: After setting a ball screen at the top of the key, the screener turns and sprints straight toward the basket with a hand up for a pass.

explanation.correct: A roll is the screener cutting toward the basket after the screen, which stretches the defense and makes the defender in the lane choose. A pop goes the other way, out to the perimeter.
explanation.incorrect: A pop means stepping out to shoot. When the screener dives to the rim for a pass, that is the roll, and it is an easy catch-and-finish if the defense lets him.

payload.prompt: Match each pick-and-roll action to what the screener does.

pairs.definition: The screener moves toward the basket after setting the screen, looking for a pass from the ball handler.
The screener steps out to the perimeter for a jump shot after the screen is set.
The screener breaks to the basket without actually setting the screen, using surprise timing.

distractorDefinitions: The ball handler fakes and goes the other direction.
The screener sets another screen at the same time.

explanation.summary: Roll is toward the basket; pop is out to shoot; slip is breaking early for a layup.

payload.prompt: Order the steps of a pick-and-roll from start to finish.

items.text: The screener moves to set a barrier for the ball handler.
The ball handler dribbles toward the screen and uses it to create space.
The screener rolls or pops, depending on how the defense plays it.
The ball handler drives, shoots or passes to the screener.

explanation.correct: The screen comes first, the handler uses it, the screener rolls or pops, and the handler makes the read. Every step depends on what the two defenders do.
explanation.incorrect: The order is screen, handler uses it, screener rolls or pops, then the handler finishes the play. The screener's move only makes sense after the screen is set.

lessons.title: Coverages: drop, hedge, switch, blitz
lessons.objective: Tell drop, hedge, switch, blitz and ice apart.

payload.prompt: Match each pick-and-roll defense to how it works.

pairs.definition: The screener's defender sinks toward the rim, protecting the basket and giving up a pull-up jumper.
The screener's defender steps out briefly to slow the ball handler, then recovers back.
The two defenders trade assignments, one guarding the new opponent.
Both defenders attack the ball handler immediately, trying to force a turnover.

distractorDefinitions: The ball handler's defender traps on the sideline.

explanation.summary: Drop protects the rim and gives up the jumper. A hedge steps out and recovers, a switch trades assignments, and a blitz sends two defenders at the ball.

payload.prompt: What is the risk of playing drop defense on a pick-and-roll?

options.text: The ball handler gets space for a pull-up jump shot.
The screener rolls unopposed for an easy layup.
The offense cannot get open for any shots.

explanation.correct: In drop, the big stays back to guard the rim, so the ball handler is left with room for a pull-up. That is a fine trade against a poor shooter and a dangerous one against a great shooter.
explanation.incorrect: Drop keeps the big near the rim, so the roller is covered. The price is space for the ball handler, who can rise up for a jumper. It is not the roller who gets loose.

payload.prompt: Match these pick-and-roll adjustments to their meanings.

pairs.definition: The defense turns the ball handler toward the sideline, away from the middle, with the big waiting to contain him.
The ball handler's defender passes behind the screener instead of fighting over it, giving up space.
The ball handler's defender fights over the top of the screen and stays attached to his man.

explanation.summary: Ice pushes the ball handler to the side. Going under gives up space to stay back, and going over keeps the defender attached.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: Hedge and recover. Do not give up the three.

payload.question: What is she calling?

options.text: The screener's defender steps out to slow the ball handler, then recovers to his own man.
Let the screener roll unopposed to the basket.
Switch defenders on the screen.
Foul the ball handler immediately.

payload.translation: She wants the big to step out and show himself to the ball handler, then get back to his own man fast, so the handler cannot shoot a three in the gap.

followUps.line: So he steps out and gets right back?
followUps.why: You are putting the coverage in plain words, which invites her to fill in the details.

followUps.line: Who recovers back to the roller?
followUps.why: A good follow-up asking who needs to be ready for the pass.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Hedge means step out and step back quickly; do not overcommit.

lessons.title: Reading a coverage live
lessons.objective: Pick the best action against each coverage as it happens.

payload.prompt: What should the ball handler do if the defense hedges tight on a pick-and-roll?

options.text: Get the ball quickly to the screener, who is briefly open.
Drive straight into the defender stepping out.
Take a long jump shot immediately.

explanation.correct: A hedge pulls the screener's defender away from the screener for a moment. A quick pass exploits that gap, because it is now a four-on-three until the defender recovers.
explanation.incorrect: The defender who steps out wants you to drive or shoot into him. The smart read is to use the gap he leaves behind and pass to the screener before he recovers.

payload.prompt: What is a short roll in a pick-and-roll?

options.text: The screener catches the ball around the free-throw line, then makes a play.
The screener dribbles a few times before shooting.
A screen set close to the ball handler's defender.

explanation.correct: On a short roll the big stops around the free-throw line and gets the pass there. With the defense still turned toward the ball handler, he can shoot, attack or pass to a shooter.
explanation.incorrect: A short roll is about where the screener catches the ball: in the middle of the floor, before the rim. It is a pass, not a dribbling move or a type of screen.

payload.question: What does that mean?

options.text: The ball handler saw how the defense played the screen and made the right pass or shot.
She studied the defense's diagram at a timeout.
She ignored the defense and did what the coach drew.
She guessed right on a risky pass.

payload.translation: The ball handler saw instantly how the defense was covering the screen (hedging, dropping, switching) and picked the best option: pass, shoot or drive.

followUps.why: It invites her to explain the coverage she saw, and you learn the name from her.
A good follow-up asking about the outcome of the smart read.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Reading coverage means seeing the defense and reacting correctly, not literally looking at diagrams.

lessons.title: Handoffs and the DHO
lessons.objective: Explain a dribble handoff and why teams love it.

payload.prompt: What is a dribble handoff (DHO)?

options.text: A dribbler hands the ball hand to hand to a teammate who is running by.
A long pass thrown across the court after a dribble.
A pass thrown into the post.

explanation.correct: In a dribble handoff, the ball goes directly from one player's hand to another's as the receiver runs past. The handler's body gets in the way of the receiver's defender, so it works like a screen.
explanation.incorrect: A handoff is not thrown at all. The ball is placed in the receiver's hands as he runs past the dribbler, which is why the two players have to be almost touching.

payload.prompt: A handler fires a pass across the lane to a cutter. Is this a handoff?

scene.alt: A ball handler throws a chest pass across the lane to a cutter who is several feet away.

explanation.correct: A handoff is hand to hand, with the two players close together. A pass across the lane is thrown, which gives the defense time to react.
explanation.incorrect: The ball is thrown across a gap here, so it is a regular pass. In a handoff the receiver takes the ball directly from the handler's hand as he passes by.

payload.prompt: Why do teams love the dribble handoff?

options.text: The handler's body can block the receiver's defender, freeing him to attack.
It forces the defense to foul more often.
It uses up the shot clock.

explanation.correct: The receiver runs by the handler and takes the ball with momentum, while the handler's body slows the receiver's defender. That defender has to chase, and the offense gets a step of space.
explanation.incorrect: The benefit is space, not fouls or clock. A handoff lets the receiver take the ball at full speed while his defender is blocked by the handler's body.

payload.prompt: Complete the dribble-handoff description.
payload.template: In a dribble handoff the ball goes {{how}} to a teammate who is {{motion}}.

explanation.correct: A handoff puts the ball straight into a moving teammate's hands. The receiver's momentum is what makes it hard for his defender to stay in front of him.
explanation.incorrect: A handoff is a hand-to-hand exchange with a teammate who is running toward the handler. Nobody is waiting in the corner or on the bench for it.

payload.prompt: Order a dribble handoff, from dribble to drive.

items.text: The handler dribbles toward a teammate.
items.why: The handler sets it up by moving the ball to the receiver.

items.text: The teammate runs toward the handler.
items.why: The receiver arrives at speed, close enough to touch.

items.text: The ball passes hand to hand as they cross.
items.why: The exchange is the handoff itself.

items.text: The receiver attacks while his defender is slowed.
items.why: The handler's body is in the way of the chase.

explanation.correct: Dribble, meet, hand the ball over, then attack. The handler's body in the way is what turns a simple exchange into an advantage.
explanation.incorrect: A handoff flows dribble, meet, exchange, attack. The exchange happens in the middle, because the defender is slowed only as the two players cross.

lessons.title: Post entries and split cuts
lessons.objective: Follow a post entry and the split cut that follows.

payload.prompt: What is a post entry?

options.text: A pass from the perimeter to a big man in the post.
A pass from the baseline to restart play.
A pass that starts a fast break.

explanation.correct: The post entry gets the ball to a big near the basket, where he can score, pass to a cutter or kick it back out. Getting the ball in safely is the hard part, because defenders try to deny it.
explanation.incorrect: A throw-in and a fast-break outlet are other passes. A post entry is the pass into the post, from the perimeter to a big who is posting up.

payload.prompt: Name the spot where the free-throw line meets the lane.
payload.template: Each {{spot}} is where the free-throw line meets the lane. It is part of the {{post}}.

explanation.correct: The elbows are the two corners of the free-throw line where it meets the lane. They are prime high-post spots: from there a big can shoot, pass or hand the ball off.
explanation.incorrect: The blocks are down near the baseline, in the low post. The elbows are the top corners of the lane at the free-throw line, which makes them part of the high post.

payload.prompt: Tap a high-post spot, near the free-throw line.

diagram.alt: Half-court diagram. The free-throw line crosses the top of the painted lane, with an elbow at each end. The blocks sit lower, beside the basket.

explanation.correct: The high post is the free-throw-line area: the two elbows and the middle between them. A big there can see the whole floor, which is why offenses run plays through it.
explanation.incorrect: That is the low post, down by the basket. The high post is the free-throw-line area: the elbows and the middle of the line.

payload.prompt: Order a split cut after a post entry.

items.text: A guard passes the ball into the big man in the post.
items.why: Everything starts with the entry pass.

items.text: The passer and a teammate cut past the big man, one on each side.
items.why: The two cutters split around the post player.

items.text: The big man reads which defender is helping or following.
items.why: He picks the pass based on the defense.

items.text: He hits an open cutter, or scores himself.
items.why: The defense cannot stop every option at once.

explanation.correct: After the entry, two players cut off the post man on either side. He watches the defense and delivers the ball to whoever is open, or scores himself.
explanation.incorrect: The order is entry pass, split cut, the big man's read, then the finish. The cut comes right after the entry, while the defense is still watching the post.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: Post entry, then kick it out.

payload.question: What is she saying?

options.text: Get the ball into the post, and if the defense collapses, pass it back out to a shooter.
Throw the ball out of bounds on purpose.
Skip the post and shoot a three right away.
Have the big man dribble the ball up the floor.

payload.translation: She wants the ball to go inside first. If the defense collapses on the big man, he passes it back out to a teammate who is now open for a three.

followUps.line: So the defense has to pick: the big or the shooters?
followUps.why: You are describing the dilemma in plain words, which shows you see why it works.

followUps.line: Who is open on the wing?
followUps.why: A good follow-up asking who the kick-out pass should go to.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Post entry is passing to a big; kick-out is passing back to a shooter when help comes.

lessons.title: Pindowns, floppy and getting shooters open
lessons.objective: Recognize the screens that free a shooter running off the ball.

payload.prompt: What is a pindown screen?

options.text: A screen for a teammate near the baseline, who runs up off it to catch and shoot.
A screen for the ball handler at the top of the key.
A screen that pins a defender against the backboard.

explanation.correct: In a pindown the screener sets his screen facing down toward the baseline, and the shooter starts low and curls up off it toward the ball. The shooter gets open for a catch-and-shoot, often at the wing or top.
explanation.incorrect: A pindown is an off-ball screen, set for a player without the ball. The screener faces the baseline and the shooter runs up off his screen, instead of a ball screen at the top.

payload.prompt: What is a stagger screen?

options.text: Two screeners set back-to-back screens, and the shooter runs off both.
One screener sets a screen and then sets another one moments later.
Two screens set for the ball handler on opposite sides.

explanation.correct: In a stagger screen two players stand one after the other, so the shooter uses both screens in a row. Two defenders get slowed, and it is hard to chase a shooter through them.
explanation.incorrect: A stagger screen has two separate screeners, set for one off-ball shooter who runs past them in turn. Two screens for the ball handler is a different action.

payload.prompt: Match each off-ball screen action to what it creates.

pairs.definition: A screen for a teammate near the baseline, who runs up off it toward the ball.
Two screeners set back-to-back screens, and the shooter runs off both.
An off-ball screen after which the shooter flares away from the ball to the wing or corner.
Two screeners in the lane let a shooter starting low choose which side to run off.

distractorDefinitions: A screen that immediately results in a foul.
A screen set in the restricted area.

explanation.summary: All four free a shooter who does not have the ball. A pindown runs him up, a stagger gives him two screens, a flare sends him away from the ball, and a floppy lets him pick a side.

payload.prompt: Tap where a flare screen sends the shooter.

diagram.alt: Half-court diagram with the basket near the bottom edge. The corners and wings sit along the sides, the top of the arc in the middle, and the lane under the basket.

explanation.correct: After a flare screen the shooter drifts away from the ball to a corner or wing, where a cross-court pass finds him open. Flare means he slides out, not in.
explanation.incorrect: A flare sends the shooter out to the side, away from the ball, toward a corner or wing. The paint and top of the key are where screens for cutters or ball handlers end up.

lessons.title: Isolation and mismatch hunting
lessons.objective: Explain why offenses force switches and attack the weak defender.

payload.prompt: Quick guard versus a slow big. Attack or reset?

situation.narrative: A ball screen forced a switch. Your quick guard has the ball against a slower big, and there is plenty of time left.

facts.label: Matchup
facts.value: Quick guard vs slow big defender

facts.label: Opportunity
facts.value: The big must guard in space

facts.label: Risk
facts.value: The big's teammates may send help

options.label: Attack the mismatch
options.consequence: The guard can drive past the big or shoot over the space he gives. Even if help comes, he has a teammate open to pass to.
considerations: The big is slower laterally than your guard
Plenty of time remains on the shot clock
If help comes, someone else is open

options.label: Reset and run a set
options.consequence: It is safe, but the defense gets time to switch back or fix the matchup, and the advantage is gone.
considerations: The mismatch disappears once the defense adjusts
It costs time on the shot clock

payload.expertNote: Offenses hunt a mismatch right away, before the defense can fix it. Coaches still weigh the help that might come, which is why a good passer is part of the plan.

payload.prompt: A great defender is on your star. What now?

situation.narrative: Your star scorer is guarded by the other team's best defender. The other team switches ball screens, and one of its bigs is slow on his feet.

facts.label: Your strength
facts.value: Star scorer with a quick first step

facts.label: Their weak link
facts.value: A slow big who would have to switch

options.label: Screen for your star to force the big to switch
options.consequence: If the defense switches, your star faces the slow big in space. If it does not, the screen still gives him a step on his defender.
considerations: A switch swaps the elite defender for a weaker one
The screen helps even when they do not switch
The defense must pick between two bad options

options.label: Clear out and let the star go one-on-one
options.consequence: A star can beat a great defender, but it is the hardest matchup to win, and the offense gets nothing extra.
considerations: It can work for a true star
It relies on a tough one-on-one shot

payload.expertNote: Offenses screen to pull the best defender away from a star or force a slow defender to switch. The plan is only as good as the coverage: against a team that does not switch, this becomes a simple ball screen.

payload.prompt: What is isolation efficiency?

options.text: The points a team scores per isolation play, one player against one defender.
How rarely a team runs isolation plays.
A count of how many players are standing still.

explanation.correct: Isolation efficiency is points per isolation possession. Analysts use it to see whether a star's one-on-one scoring is actually a good way to score, compared with other plays.
explanation.incorrect: It is not a count of plays or standing players. Isolation efficiency is the points per isolation possession, which is what tells you if iso ball is working.

payload.prompt: Why might a team choose to switch everything on defense?

options.text: Screens stop freeing shooters, even though size mismatches appear.
It lets the offense cut to the rim without being guarded.
It guarantees every defender stays with his original man.

explanation.correct: When every defender switches, nobody has to chase a shooter around a screen, so open threes get rarer. The price is that a big may end up on a quick guard, or a small on a big, so teams need switchable players.
explanation.incorrect: Switching means defenders trade men, so nobody stays with his original man. The point is to stay attached to shooters through screens, and the trade-off is size mismatches.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: They keep hunting us on the switch. We need to go big.

payload.question: What is she saying?

options.text: The other team forces switches to pick on a smaller defender; she wants a bigger lineup.
Her team should stop switching and play zone.
Her team should shoot more threes.
Her team should slow the pace down.

payload.translation: The other team keeps running screens to get a smaller defender switched onto their best players, and she thinks her team should play taller players so those matchups stop hurting them.

followUps.why: It lets her tell you which player she has in mind, and it invites her to explain the matchup.

followUps.line: Is it their guard or their big causing it?
followUps.why: It shows you know a mismatch has two sides and asks her to name the weak spot.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Hunting switches means using screens to get a weak defender on a star. Going big just means playing taller players. You can ask which matchup she means.

lessons.title: Late-clock offense
lessons.objective: Understand the 14-second reset and what teams do as the shot clock runs down.

payload.prompt: Bar runs 24 to 0. Tap to attack with 8 to 5 seconds left.

explanation.correct: Offenses try to start the real attack with roughly 8 to 5 seconds left, so a drive, a kick and a shot all fit. That is a rule of thumb, not a rule.
explanation.incorrect: Start too early and the set may not be over, and start too late and there is no time for a second pass. Around 8 to 5 seconds is where late-clock attacks usually begin.

payload.prompt: When an offensive rebound is grabbed in the NBA, what happens to the shot clock?

options.text: It resets to 14 seconds, giving the offense a second chance with less time.
It resets to 24 seconds, the same as the start of a possession.
It stops and does not reset.

explanation.correct: Exactly. The 14-second reset is a key rule: grab an offensive board, get 14 seconds to shoot again. Great chance to score.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Offensive rebounds reset the shot clock to 14 seconds in the NBA, giving a quick second chance.

payload.prompt: What is a bailout shot?

options.text: A late-clock desperation shot taken when the play breaks down and time is almost out.
A free throw awarded after a team fouls out.
A game-winning shot by a bench player.

explanation.correct: A bailout shot is a rushed attempt when the possession has broken down and the clock is almost out. It is often a contested three or a long two, taken because nothing better is left.
explanation.incorrect: A bailout shot is not a foul-out free throw or a comeback shot. It is what a team throws up at the end of the shot clock when the offense has not produced a good look.

payload.prompt: Bar runs 24 to 0. Tap to get a shot up by 3 to 1 seconds.

explanation.correct: With about three seconds left there is time for one move and one shot. Waiting longer risks a shot-clock violation, because the ball must leave the hand, and hit the rim, before zero.
explanation.incorrect: Tap too soon and the shot is rushed, and tap too late and the shot clock expires. Around three to one seconds left is the last window to get a shot off safely.

payload.prompt: If an offensive rebound happens with 3 seconds left on the shot clock, how much time do you get to shoot?

explanation.correct: After an offensive rebound the NBA shot clock resets to 14 seconds, even when the old clock was almost out. A team that grabs its own miss gets a fresh, shorter possession.
explanation.incorrect: The clock does not keep its three seconds or go back to 24. An NBA offensive rebound resets it to 14, enough for one more good try.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: Late clock. Just give it to him and clear out.

payload.question: What is she saying?

options.text: With the shot clock nearly gone, let one player create a shot one-on-one.
Call a timeout before the clock runs out.
Pass the ball to the bench.
Slow the game down even more.

payload.translation: With only a few seconds left on the shot clock, there is no time for a play. She wants the best scorer to take the ball, teammates to spread out, and him to make something happen.

followUps.line: So it is all on him at that point?
followUps.why: You are checking your understanding in plain words, and she gets to explain why late-clock iso is such a gamble.
A good follow-up asking if the iso player got space for a shot.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Late-clock iso just means the offense ran out of time, so one player takes over. No jargon beyond that is needed.
